text: I read the supplied files. Q is Struski et al., Competitive Market Behavior of LLMs (double auction); P is a CVaR resource-allocation mechanism note whose Section 1 calls Garjani et al. "Q" and Wang et al. "P". I will treat the supplied files as the assigned pair, flag that internal cross-reference mismatch, and investigate whether P\(\)\(\)s tail-risk framework sharpens Q\(\)\(\)s finite-horizon trade-completion result. Q Method: 5 rounds, at most 300 iterations, no-trade profit zero; Q Results: GPT Large makes one-cent improvements and trades only 2.2–3.8 times per round. P Sections 3–4 concern expected empirical CVaR surrogates and warn that one sample can select a true-risk-worse action.

Initial intersection: Q Sections 3.2-3.3 give a finite-horizon order book where crossing a standing quote locks in profit and a noncrossing improvement may earn more later or yield zero; Q Section 4.1 attributes low GPT Large efficiency to delayed crossing. P Sections 2-4 distinguish true CVaR from expected fixed-batch empirical CVaR and show a surrogate equilibrium can fail true-risk participation. Intention: derive a minimal cross-versus-wait example inside Q rules where exact fixed-batch CVaR optimization favors waiting but true CVaR favors immediate crossing. This would be a conditional mechanism, not an explanation of Q observations, since Q agents were instructed to maximize profit and no CVaR estimator is reported.

Alternative to Emmy\(\)s fixed-batch action example: P Section 4 explicitly distinguishes sums of local CVaRs from CVaR of aggregate loss. Q Section 4.1 reports only per-round means across 10 independent runs, although a stalled market is a downside event. Sharpened question: can a finite-horizon CDA intervention improve CVaR of market-wide efficiency loss, rather than just mean trade count or individual CVaR? For Q round-5 GPT Small mean efficiency 0.91, efficiency means alone permit ten run values all 0.91 or nine values 1 and one 0.1; with loss \(L=1-E\), their empirical upper-tail \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.1}(L)\) is 0.09 versus 0.9. Other table marginals may constrain examples, but cannot identify a joint tail. A 5% failure event is missed in 10 independent runs with probability \(0.95^{10}\approx0.599\). P Section 4 bound is for expected empirical surrogate, not confidence for a realised sample. Prior work already studies risk-based CDA bidding (Vytelingum et al. 2004, https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/259567/), so generic risk bidding is not a novelty claim.

Candidate exact bridge (Q Method, Trading Mechanism and Information/Objective; P Sections 2-4). At a Q penultimate iteration with no previous trades, let a buyer have value \(v=3.25\), standing ask \(a=3.00\), and an improvable bid \(b=2.25<a\). Crossing earns sure profit \(g=v-a=0.25\). Posting \(b\) can earn \(h=v-b=1\) if one of the seven sellers with reservation value at most \(2.25\) is selected next and crosses; under that stipulated continuation policy and Q uniform selection among 22 untraded agents, success probability is \(p=7/22\), otherwise profit is zero at the cap. For upper-tail CVaR of loss with tail mass \(\beta=1/2\), true risk-adjusted utility of waiting is zero (failure probability \(15/22>\beta\)), below crossing utility \(1/4\). With one observation, expected empirical CVaR equals expected loss, giving surrogate waiting utility \(7/22>1/4\); with two observations the surrogate waiting utility is \((7/22)^2<1/4\). Thus batch size alone flips the exact two-action choice. This is a constructed state/policy, not Q empirical behavior or a theorem about LLM agents. I will write the general binomial derivation and limits in emmy/.

I wrote a detailed note at ada/cvar_cda_note.tex. Conditional decision result using Q Sections 3.2-3.3 and P Section 2 CVaR: if crossing a profitable standing quote gives certain profit \(r>0\), while a specified noncrossing continuation has nonnegative eventual profit \(W\) with \(\Pr(W=0)\geq\beta\), then \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{\beta}(-W)=0>-r=\operatorname{CVaR}_{\beta}(-r)\); a local CVaR minimizer crosses. In a two-point continuation \(W=h\) with probability \(p\), mean-profit maximization waits when \(ph>r\), whereas tail-risk minimization crosses when \(\beta\leq1-p\). Q did not elicit CVaR preferences or counterfactual \(p\), so this is a testable mechanism, not an explanation of its agents. More crossing need not improve Q\(\)s allocative efficiency: a buyer valued at 2.25 crossing a seller at ask 1/cost .75 realizes surplus 1.5, while a later buyer valued 3.25 could realize 2.5 with that seller. This is the local-versus-aggregate risk distinction P Section 4 cautions about.

Cross-check of Emmy entry #4: Q\(\)s 11 seller reservation values on \([0.75,3.25]\) in 0.25 steps include exactly seven at or below 2.25; Q selects uniformly among 22 untraded agents, and a seller ask at or below standing bid 2.25 executes at that bid. Thus the stipulated one-step fill probability \(p=7/22\) is internally consistent if each such seller crosses and all other selected agents do not execute. For \(h=1,r=1/4,\beta=1/2\), true waiting CVaR utility is 0 because \(1-p=15/22>1/2\), whereas one-sample expected empirical utility is \(p=7/22>1/4\) and two-sample is \(p^2=49/484<1/4\). Caveat: the policy of other agents is constructed, and the stationary best bid/ask and no prior trades must be specified; no observed Q behaviour or strategic equilibrium follows. My #5 establishes the general threshold; Emmy\(\)s exact Q-state example makes the fixed-batch bias more pair-specific. The research test still needs aggregate surplus, since local CVaR crossing can displace a higher-value buyer.

Correction to my #5/#6 and ada/cvar_cda_note.tex: the low-value-buyer crossing example is an allocation-displacement externality, not itself P Section 4\(\)s nonadditivity of CVaR. P\(\)s \(\sum_i\operatorname{CVaR}(J_i)\neq\operatorname{CVaR}(\sum_i J_i)\) supplies a separate reason local risk optimization need not control market-wide tail risk. Both limitations matter for a Q-style experiment; they should not be conflated.

Prior-work check narrows any novelty claim. Search queries: "conditional value at risk continuous double auction strategic bidding trade execution risk aversion paper", "large language model agents double auction risk aversion CVaR market efficiency", "CVaR continuous double auction agent bidding", and "LLM CVaR double auction". Vytelingum et al. 2004 already propose risk-based CDA bidding (https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/259567/); Panda et al. 2019 use CVaR in double-auctioned power-market bidding (https://doi.org/10.1049/iet-gtd.2018.5905). I found no directly matching LLM finite-horizon CVaR execution test in those queries, but this is no novelty claim. The threshold in #5 is elementary; a publishable contribution would need controlled LLM-market evidence on both market-level tail inefficiency and allocation displacement. Updated ada/cvar_cda_note.tex accordingly.

Derivation and limits now in emmy/cross_wait.md. General two-point result: crossing gives sure \(g>0\); noncrossing bid gives \(h>g\) with probability \(p\), zero otherwise. For loss \(L=-\pi\), tail mass \(\beta\), and \(f=1-p\), true risk utility is \(h(1-f/\beta)_+\); expected empirical utility from batch size \(s\) is \(h\mathbb E[(1-M/(\beta s))_+]\), \(M\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(s,f)\). Thus \(s=1\) is expected profit \(ph\), and with \(\beta=1/2\), \(s=2\) is \(p^2h\). More generally expected empirical CVaR of any integrable loss is downward biased, since \(\mathbb E\inf_\eta F_s(\eta)\leq\inf_\eta\mathbb EF_s(\eta)\). The Q-grid instance in #4 changes from wait to cross between one and two samples; with an ask from cost-\(1\) seller and no other trades, crossing welfare is \(9/4\) versus waiting expected welfare \(49/88\). This welfare comparison is conditional; Ada #5 correctly warns that crossing can displace higher-value buyers in other states. Prior risk-based CDA bidding: https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/259567/ ; sampling CVaR bias work: https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v29i1.9561 . Search queries and detailed source passages are in the note. No novelty claim for either generic ingredient.

Cross-check of Emmy #9 welfare arithmetic: for the seven seller costs \(c\in\{0.75,1,1.25,1.5,1.75,2,2.25\}\), \(\sum_c(3.25-c)/22=(7\cdot3.25-10.5)/22=49/88\). Crossing the cost-1 standing seller gives \(3.25-1=9/4\), so the constructed one-step state has higher expected welfare under immediate crossing. This does not contradict my displacement state: the sign of welfare change depends on which future counterparties are displaced. The proposed paper should make that sign a measured outcome, not assume it from local CVaR or higher trade count.

Experimental-design correction to #9 and emmy/cross_wait.md: the reversal \(7/22>1/4\) is for the optimizer of the *expected* one-sample empirical CVaR, matching P Section 2. It does not predict a deterministic wait choice after one realised sample; with a realised one-sample outcome, a sample-based chooser waits on a sampled fill and crosses on a sampled failure. A matched-state study should first use many continuation rollouts under fixed other-agent policies to estimate each action distribution and compute the expected fixed-batch oracle. Only then test an LLM intervention using averaged outputs over repeated fresh batches of chosen size, followed by full-market outcomes. This is necessary to identify the P-style surrogate effect separately from realised-sample randomness.

Information caveat for Emmy #4/#9: Q Information and Objective gives each agent only its own reservation value, book, and histories, not the other seven sellers\(\) private costs. The analyst can compute \(p=7/22\) from Q\(\)s full experimental design plus a stipulated seller policy, but a Q trader cannot generally know that probability at this state. The example is an oracle-backed counterfactual within Q\(\)s trading rules, not an implementable decision rule for the paper\(\)s prompted agents unless one specifies an information-respecting learned belief or supplies a sampling oracle. A decisive experiment should distinguish oracle access from publicly inferable fill-probability estimates.

Further transfer limit: P\(\)s Section 4 value-error guarantee assumes bounded, Lipschitz local CVaR on valid perturbed feasible points and an exact equilibrium of a quadratic tax game. Q\(\)s cross-versus-quote action is discrete, matching is discontinuous at the spread, and its LLM traders use no quadratic tax game or empirical-CVaR oracle. The two-action CVaR calculation is valid directly from the risk definition, but P\(\)s convergence and \(2e_n\) welfare/participation guarantees cannot simply be attached to Q. Q\(\)s ten evaluation runs are also distinct from a trader\(\)s CVaR batch size \(s\).

Best account of this assigned pair: Q (Trading Mechanism; Information and Objective; Market-Wide Outcomes) supplies a finite-horizon CDA with sure profitable spread crossing, possible zero-profit nonfill, and observed GPT Large stalling. Supplied P (fixed-batch failure; conditional guarantees; Interpretation) supplies the warning that optimizing expected empirical CVaR can select a true-risk-worse action, and distinguishes local from aggregate risk. Emmy #4/#9 gives the exact within-Q-rules two-action counterfactual where an expected one-sample CVaR surrogate waits although true CVaR crosses; I checked its probability and welfare arithmetic in #6/#10. My contribution is the general crossing threshold and a market-level check: even true local CVaR crossing can displace more valuable traders, and Q\(\)s ten-run means do not identify downside efficiency. A plausible publication question is whether information-respecting, tail-risk-aware execution improves market-wide tail surplus in Q\(\)s CDA, and whether fixed batches reverse that effect. Current evidence is a constructed state plus diagnostic calculations, not an observed LLM effect or priority claim. Unresolved: realistic belief/oracle access under Q\(\)s private information, action-specific continuation distributions, batch-size intervention, aggregate welfare and tail estimates with adequate independent runs, and literature coverage beyond the recorded queries. P\(\)s quadratic-tax equilibrium bounds and algorithm do not transfer directly.

Current judgement after Ada #12-13 and cross-check: the defensible joint lead is the conditional late-CDA ranking reversal in emmy/cross_wait.md, not a claim about Q's observed LLM objective or P's quadratic-mechanism theorem. Q tells traders only own reservation, book, and history (Q.tex lines 261-278), so the seven low-cost sellers and \(p=7/22\) are analyst information; an oracle or information-respecting belief estimator must be specified. Q's agents were instructed to maximize profit, and \(s=1\) expected empirical CVaR chooses exactly the expected-profit action here, so this example alone cannot explain their behavior. P's Section 4 equilibrium, smoothing, and welfare bounds do not transfer to a discontinuous CDA; the two-action value comparison is derived directly. Ada's aggregate-risk and allocation-displacement objections are separate and valid. A paper would need matched-state counterfactual rollouts, oracle versus public-history arms, and full-market surplus/tail-risk measurements. The pair alone supplies a precise hypothesis and a small proposition, not empirical confirmation or a novelty claim.

After Emmy #16, I rechecked Q.tex lines 239-278 and P.tex lines 28-64. The strict crossing reversal is a valid conditional two-action result: (p h>g>0) and (Pr(W=0)geq eta) make the one-sample expected empirical CVaR surrogate prefer waiting while true CVaR prefers crossing. It is not P\(\)s participation failure: waiting has true risk utility zero, not negative utility relative to opting out. The all-untraded penultimate state in Emmy #4 is allowed by Q\(\)s rules but not shown to occur in its runs. A first empirical gate is to count reachable late states whose rollout-estimated action distributions satisfy the reversal inequalities under fixed other-agent policies, then compare hidden-state oracle and public-history beliefs. If such states are rare, this constructed proposition alone gives little publication case. Aggregate welfare and its tail remain separate outcomes.
Correction to #17: the two inequalities should read \(ph>g>0\) and \(\Pr(W=0)\geq\beta\). The mathematical content and caveats of #17 are unchanged; its formula markup was mangled in transmission.

I accept Ada #17 and updated emmy/cross_wait.md accordingly. The result is an action-ranking reversal, not P's negative-participation example: true-risk utility of waiting is \(0\), equal to no trade, while crossing yields \(1/4\). The first empirical gate should count reachable late Q states whose rollout-estimated action distributions satisfy \(ph>g>h(1-f/\beta)_+\); a low prevalence would weaken the publication case. This gate precedes any claim about full-market tail surplus or LLM behaviour.
